scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pungmul is rooted in the dure collective labor farming culture, rural holidays, community-building events, and shamanistic rituals.
During the Japanese colonial era (1910–1945), colonial authorities promoted the term nongak to limit its scope and suppress its cultural meaning.
In the late 1960s and 1970s, it gained new life in political protests during the pro-democracy movement.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically played during farm work, lunar holidays, village community events, shamanistic rituals, and fundraising.
In the late 20th century, it became an important artistic medium for political protest and expression during the pro-democracy movement.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Most performances take place outdoors with dozens of players in constant motion, featuring group formations (jinpuri), solo performances by the lead gong player (Sangsoe Noleum), hat-streamer twirling (Sangmonori), hourglass drum solos (Suljanggu Noleum), small drum dances (Sogo Noleum), and satirical character skits (japsaek).
Watch for Sangmonori, Sogo Noleum.

Formation: Outdoor processions and dynamic group formations (jinpuri)

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Drumming is the central element of pungmul, utilizing five major instruments: the kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), jing (gong), and sogo (small handle drum).
Wind instruments such as the taepyeongso (hojeok, senap, or nalari) also accompany the drummers.
Listen for the kkwaenggwari, janggu, buk, jing.

A thunderous, highly dynamic percussion landscape driven by the piercing metallic ring of the kkwaenggwari gong, the resonant low thud of the buk barrel drum, the complex pitch bends of the janggu hourglass drum, and the deep reverberation of the jing gong.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Sim U-seong, Kim Swoo Geun, Kim Bong Jun, and Yi Jong-hun.

Recognized in five primary regional styles under South Korean cultural property designation: Jinju Samcheonpo nongak (yeongnam style), Pyeongtaek nongak (utdari style), Iri nongak (honam udo style), Gangneung nongak (yeongdong style), and Imsil Pilbong nongak (honam jwado style, known for rapid rhythms and varying formations).
Rooted in ancient agricultural and shamanistic traditions; gave rise to modern staged percussion genres like SamulNori and shares historical ties with itinerant Namsadang troupes.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Pungmul is child of SamulNori: Traditional percussion genre derived from multiple pungmul styles, performed seated.
Pungmul is sibling of Namsadang: Itinerant performance troupe having pungmul in its repertoire.
Pungmul is shares music of Pung cholom: A similar dance from Manipur, India.
